paragraphs.text: Chapter 1. Sleep

Sleep is the subject of the first chapter of this book because sleep profoundly impacts every aspect of our physiology and psychology. Put simply, sleep is the foundation of our mental health, our physical health, and our performance. [^1] We win by sleeping.

I came to that realization pretty early but only because I struggled with sleep. As a kid I slept like a log—always a solid eight to nine hours, rarely waking up in the middle of the night even once. As a teen I would stay out late and sleep in on the weekends, as most of us did. I never thought about my sleep.

When I reached my junior year in high school, however, everything changed. I would lie down, fall asleep right away, but then wake up three to four hours later, wide awake. Then I would toss and turn. Eventually I would fall back asleep but then needed to sleep really late into the morning to feel rested. School started at 8:00 a.m., so that wasn’t an option most days. That had me falling asleep in class, feeling wide awake in the evening, and then the whole cycle would repeat.

Toward the end of high school when I started getting into fitness, I learned that we recover from exercise during sleep. That was the early 1990s and the public was not yet aware of the importance of sleep. There was some science on it—in fact some of the best work on the role of sleep for health and cognition was coming from the Stanford Sleep Lab just a few miles up the road from where I lived. But it was from a prominent trainer in the world of fitness that I first learned to take sleep seriously. He gave me one mostly good suggestion for sleep, and one terrible one. The mostly good suggestion was to read the work of Allan Hobson—a sleep researcher from Harvard—and I eventually did, although I discovered Allan’s focus was mainly on the importance of dreams, which felt like a bit of a tease for someone with sleep issues. The terrible advice he gave me? He told me if I woke up in the middle of the night and couldn’t fall back asleep that I should drink a half mug of white wine. I was seventeen! I tried it anyway, and it didn’t work for me. Thankfully. We now know alcohol greatly reduces the quality and restorative properties of sleep, even if it does help some people fall asleep.

Eventually I figured out how to master the art of getting a great night’s sleep, but it took time. Years, in fact. The science progressed too, of course, and we now know a lot about both the importance of sleep and ways to remedy pretty much any sleep issue. I wish I had the information you are about to read back in high school, and college, and graduate school, and my postdoc. The reality is, the busier we are, the more important sleep is to our health and performance. But no matter how busy or calm our life is, a great night’s sleep is crucial to our mind and body.

If you are like the majority of people, and you struggle to get a great night’s sleep, you want to remedy that as soon as possible. [^2] But even if you are one of those rare individuals who sleeps deeply every night and wakes up feeling fully refreshed every day, there are still ways to improve your sleep and thus, your quality of life. Regardless of which category you fall into, this chapter will help.

I’d like to mention here that this chapter is a long one. We go deep into the science of sleep, but I promise you it’s all made accessible. I know that understanding this science will help you get a great night’s sleep. I wrote this chapter so you can browse by topic or tool. Start with the parts that interest you most, or the protocols that you think will help you right now.

I prefer to focus on the benefits of doing things correctly, but when it comes to sleep, it’s worth thinking a bit about the downsides of getting things wrong too, and learning to avoid those. Sleep deprivation—a term that means getting too little sleep or waking up too many times during the night—has been linked to significantly elevated risk of heart disease, stroke, and numerous hormonal imbalances involving—just to name a handful: cortisol, estrogen, testosterone, and insulin, the latter of which can cause type 2 diabetes. [^3] Obesity, mental health issues, physical injuries, cancer, car accidents, depression, hypertension, and age-related dementia have all also been linked to poor sleep. [^4] Sleep deprivation doesn’t necessarily directly create these problems; rather it impairs cellular mechanisms that cascade to produce multiple issues within and between different organs and systems.

To be clear, everyone has a bad night’s sleep now and again. But here’s a good goal for you: Aim to sleep well 90 to 95 percent of the nights of your life, and allow the remaining 5 to 10 percent of those nights to be bad due to uncontrollable negative circumstances, like a work conflict, or joyful experiences, like a great party. Do your best to make sleep a top priority so that the rest of your life can be that much better.

Perhaps you have heard some of this before. Most people know a bit about the benefits and importance of sleep. As I mentioned above, that is a fairly recent development. It was about a decade ago when Matthew Walker, who formerly directed the Center for Human Sleep Science at the University of California, Berkeley, and is currently at the University of Texas in Dallas, wrote the now famous book, Why We Sleep. At that time, the “I’ll sleep when I’m dead” or the “I’ll catch up on sleep this weekend” mentalities prevailed. [^5] Thanks in large part to Matt’s book and other public education efforts, people now recognize they must sleep, yet the majority of people still don’t sleep well and far too many people sleep poorly, with nearly half of adults reporting their sleep satisfaction as an “F”—meaning the lowest possible grade. [^6] It is true that we all have slightly different sleep needs. Some of us consider ourselves morning larks. We prefer to rise early. Others are night owls who prefer to stay up late. These are what sleep researchers call chronotypes: genetically determined features of the chemicals, cells, and circuits that regulate when we prefer to go to sleep and wake up. You can blame your parents for your bedtime (and wake time) preference.

Separate from your chronotype is the total amount of sleep you need. Some of us need six hours to feel fully rested, others need eight, and some people feel great with just five. I should point out, however, that the feel-great-on-five folks are exceedingly rare. Most people need seven to eight. [^7] But as mentioned above, according to recent reports from the National Sleep Foundation and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), at least a third of Americans do not get nearly enough sleep—and that statistic is likely to be a vast underestimate given the enormous increase in time spent on social media and online nowadays. [^8] In fact, that figure skyrockets to more than 75 percent among high school students. That’s right, approximately three-fourths of teens are not getting enough sleep, [^9] which is extremely concerning given that our adolescent and teen years are when much of our brain wiring related to mood and behavior regulation, as well as attention and learning, gets solidified. From birth until about age twenty-five is an especially sensitive and time-limited phase, or what is called a critical period. [^10] And the thing about critical periods is eventually they close: While our brains remain plastic our entire lives, the amount of neuroplasticity possible in those first twenty-five years far exceeds what is possible afterward, so teens can’t simply make up for their lost brain wiring later on. [^11] We have no idea what the long-term consequences of this kind of chronic sleep deprivation are, but we do know that far too many young people are missing out on sleep at exactly the time when they need it most.

Compulsive overuse of phones and other screen-based technologies at night is a major factor for the poor sleep of adolescents and teens, but also for the poor sleep habits of adults. [^12] A central feature of life in the twenty-first century is to always be connected online and by text. So much so that by the classic definition of shift work, many—perhaps even most people—worldwide, now meet the definition of a shift worker, that is, awake for two to three hours between 10:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m. Shift work is not just about staying up late but also involves reduced amounts of exposure to sunlight during the day, lack of sufficient darkness at night, and a nocturally-shifted eating schedule. That has well-established negative health effects, including poor gut health, mental health deficits, and even decreased lifespan. [^13] So this is no trivial matter. Smartphone technologies are not to blame per se, but when we use those technologies certainly is. We can scroll 24-7 and unless we resist, the light from our phone, tablet, or computer screen impairs our sleep. Not to mention that the content we absorb on those screens often affects our sleep, too, because of the elevated levels of arousal—aka stress—that content creates. Even if being on our phones or tablets in the hours before sleep doesn’t stress us out, it can disrupt our sleep. [^14] We rarely hear how texting alters our sleep patterns but I would argue that for many people, it is at least as pernicious as social media in this regard. To be clear, texting is a wonderful tool for communication; it allows us to connect quickly. And social media can be a good source for learning, social connection, and entertainment. The downside, however, is that we can have conversations and observe events at any time of day or night. If we wake up in the middle of the night, we know we should roll over and go back to sleep, but many of us instead start reading and sending texts, or scrolling the internet or browsing social media.

So it comes as no surprise that most of us now qualify as shift workers but very few of us are sacrificing our sleep hours by doing actual work. [^15] We have all become so habituated to this new normal of consuming content and communicating at all hours that we don’t see how out of sync it really is with our sleep and therefore our health.
The good news is, we can fix our sleep duration, quality, and even determine its timing—regardless of our chronotype—without having to disengage too much from these technologies.

And it’s oh-so-worth it because when I say, “We win by sleeping,” I am referring to the fact that sleep shapes everything about us—how we look, how we think, and how we feel. But I also mean that if you get your sleep right 90 percent of the time, you’ll be absolutely amazed how your appearance, health, and performance will improve. The data say you’ll likely live longer as well. [^16]

This chapter offers protocols you can easily integrate into your life to get far more restful and restorative sleep. That is, to “sleep better.” None take much time, and many of them are downright pleasurable. Let’s consider these protocols in order of their importance.
SLEEP PROTOCOL 1 View Sunlight as Soon as Possible After Waking
WHAT TO DO

• Get morning sunlight in your eyes as soon as possible after waking. Go outside and look in the direction of the sun for at least five to ten minutes each morning. Your goal should be to get sunlight in your eyes within the first thirty to sixty minutes of waking up.

• A few things to keep in mind. If you wake up before the sun rises, you’ll obviously have to wait. If you can view the sun as it comes up across the horizon, great, but that’s not vital for this protocol to work. Morning sunlight, as we will review, differs in quality from sunlight at other times of the day. It is best viewed by facing the sun without any physical barriers, like awnings or buildings, obscuring your view. Don’t wear a brimmed hat, as it blocks some of the light that would otherwise reach your eyes from overhead. Wearing eyeglasses or contacts is fine but, alas, this protocol won’t work nearly as well through a window or windshield, as that will filter out many of the relevant wavelengths of light. Skip the sunglasses while doing this protocol. What about clouds? No matter how overcast, there is always some sunlight coming through once the sun is up. In fact, the more accurate way to state this protocol would be “get as-early-in-your-day-as-possible daylight in your eyes,” but that is a mouthful. The point is that the sun provides daylight even on overcast days. Just compare how bright it is at 8:00 a.m. on an overcast day to midnight the night before. So forget the “there is no sun out in winter where I live” argument. There is daylight, and you want to view it. Indeed, this protocol is especially important on cloudy days. Caution: Do not stare at the sun. Never force your eyes to stay open. Allow your natural squint and blink reflexes to protect your eyes. If the sun still feels too bright, look a few degrees to the side of the sun.
HOW IT WORKS

Correctly timed sunlight viewing—especially morning sunlight viewing—is immensely beneficial to our overall health. This simple, zero-cost protocol powerfully affects your daytime mood, focus, and alertness, and improves your sleep, which further improves your health and performance in myriad ways.

The power of this protocol arises from its impact on three synergistic elements: your circadian clock, your eyes (or more specifically, the nerve cells in your eyes that detect sunlight and communicate its presence to your circadian clock), and specific qualities of light that come from the sun, especially when it is low, relative to the horizon. Together, these three elements make up a robust network that drives many of the biological processes in your brain and body.

I first learned about the importance of viewing morning sunlight from one of the world’s preeminent sleep researchers, Seiji Nishino, MD, PhD. I was working in his lab at Stanford during a summer home from college, and I noticed he would always stop to face the sun for a few minutes before going into the lab for the day. Even if he arrived at the lab before sunrise (not uncommon for researchers in a sleep lab!), he would make sure to step outside shortly after sunrise and face the sun for a few minutes before returning to work. That was way back in 1996—when our understanding of the mechanisms of human circadian biology was rudimentary compared to now. Seiji explained that viewing morning sunlight felt good, that it gave him more energy for the day, and that it improved his sleep. I started joining him and joked that we resembled the many ground squirrels around us up on their haunches doing the very same thing. Little did I know that the exact same morning sunlight-sensing cells, circuits, and mechanisms were at play in us and those squirrels and, in fact, in every mammal where they have been examined.

I quickly noticed that on days I viewed morning sunlight, I also felt good, had more energy for the day, and slept better at night, so I kept with it. You should experience those benefits, too, because of the way morning sunlight—whether on a clear or cloudy day—kickstarts a powerful set of hormonal and neural mechanisms that positively shift the state of your entire brain and body for many hours afterward. It can work the first time and every time, and once you understand a bit about those mechanisms, it will allow you to easily adjust this protocol to your schedule and circumstances to derive the maximum benefits with minimal time investment.
Your Circadian Clock

Located a few centimeters above the roof of your mouth is a small cluster of neurons called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, or SCN. [^17] The SCN is your master circadian clock. Its job is to coordinate the activities of all the cells and organs in your body into a coherent twenty-four-hour rhythm so that certain cells and organs in your body are more active, and other cells and organs are less active, depending on the phase of that twenty-four-hour rhythm. The SCN keeps your body and brain on schedule.

The first documented discovery of a circadian clock came not from studies of humans or even of rodents, but of plants. In 1729, a French astronomer named Jean-Jacques d’Ortous de Mairan noticed that a mimosa plant kept in a totally dark room continued to rhythmically fold and unfold its leaves every twenty-four hours, just as if the sun was shining through the window. [^18] It was a mystery: If the plant was not unfurling to absorb sun or other light, then what was guiding its movements? About two hundred years later, German biologist Erwin Bünning tracked the movements of bean plant leaves and reported that they followed a cycle lasting 24.4 hours. Observations such as these confirmed that plants had internal, or what scientists call “endogenous,” clocks that followed what later became known as… a circadian rhythm, named for the Latin circa diem, or “around a day.” And as decades of research would eventually confirm, the vast majority of organisms on Earth—not just plants but also insects, rodents, reptiles, and all mammals, including humans—have an endogenous timekeeper that keeps a twenty-four-hour circadian rhythm, even in the absence of any external cues about the status of the outside world. [^19]

Our core body temperature, the release of certain hormones, and most notably our sleep-wake cycle, all follow a twenty-four-hour circadian rhythm. [^20] Even when scientists extracted individual cells from the body, the cells continued to follow this rhythm. [^21] And which genes they expressed and when, the proteins downstream of those genes, the cells’ enzymatic activities—indeed not just some things but nearly everything about cellular function—appeared to vary, not randomly, but rather systematically every twenty-four hours. That was remarkable.

But what is equally remarkable is that all cells in our body can coordinate their individual rhythms in a manner that is timed perfectly with one another—like a well-practiced symphony, except this symphony involves not a few hundred or even a thousand participants, but trillions. And just like a symphony, it is not as if every cell simply needs to start and end its activity at the same time. Some cells need to be active at the same time, or in-phase with one another; some need to be active at opposite times, or in anti-phase, and still others repeat their cycles of activity faster, then slower, then faster, again with a unique signature and yet, still repeating once every twenty-four hours. And the start and end time of each cell’s twenty-four-hour rhythm must be tightly bound to all the other cells of the body, just like the start and end of a symphony. Without this coordination, you end up with noise rather than music, illness rather than wellness. The only difference is the symphony that is your physiology never ceases; it repeats every twenty-four hours, from the day you’re born until the day you die.

The basis of that persistent and extraordinarily precise biological coordination remained a mystery until somewhat recently. Clues came from multiple sources. First, studies in which people were placed into constant dark environments—such as caves or windowless bunkers—confirmed the existence of a circadian rhythm in humans. Back in 1938, two physiologists spent a month in Mammoth Cave, Kentucky (perhaps figuring this experiment was best done on themselves before asking anyone else to try it). [^22] There, they confirmed that human body temperature has a circadian rhythm whereby it increases upon waking, decreases approximately ten to twelve hours later, drops to its nadir during sleep, then rises once again—all once every twenty-four hours, even though the subjects/researchers had no access to sunlight or other cues about time of day. And other studies confirmed that, in the absence of an alternating pattern of ambient light and darkness, the human body still maintains a circadian rhythm for numerous aspects of our physiology. [^23]

In 1966, a German physician named Jürgen Aschoff initiated what became known as the bunker experiment, in which subjects (not researchers this time!) spent several weeks in a sealed bunker, living life as usual but without any windows or other ways to determine the passage of time. [^24] They found that subjects generally spent about one-third of each twenty-four-hour period sleeping and two-thirds of it awake, just as most humans living aboveground do. However, the wake-up and to-sleep times of the people in the bunker drifted—they woke up slightly later and went to sleep slightly later each day. Thus, the bunker experiment confirmed the existence of a circadian rhythm, but one that requires some external cue to anchor it. What remained mysterious was the biological basis of the circadian clock—was it a bloodborne factor? In the liver? In the brain? In the pineal gland? Theories abounded but none of them held up to experimentation. And another major question remained: In the environment outside the bunker, which external cues were responsible for setting that clock to a specific start and finish time each day?

Subsequent discoveries, first in rodents and later in humans, revealed the existence of a small cluster—or what is called a “nucleus”—of neurons located a few centimeters above our mouths that had a key part to play. It was later named the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) for “above the chiasm”—the chiasm being the location at the base of the brain where the nerve fibers from both eyes partially cross. As I mentioned earlier, the SCN is the master circadian clock: the structure that coordinates the activities of all our cells and organs. In other words, the SCN is the orchestra conductor that makes sure each cell’s twenty-four-hour rhythm starts on time. [^25] In 1972, Irving Zucker’s lab at UC Berkeley and Robert Moore’s lab at the University of Chicago independently discovered that lesions to the SCN render organisms’ circadian pattern arrhythmic and disorganized. [^26] Naturally occurring SCN lesions caused by tumors eventually showed the SCN is necessary for sleep-wake, hunger, and other bodily rhythms to obey circadian cycles in humans as well. [^27] Moreover, animal studies showed that transplanting even just a small number of healthy SCN neurons into an arrhythmic brain restored a coherent twenty-four-hour rhythm, proving the SCN is both necessary and sufficient for endogenous circadian rhythms. [^28]

If ever there was a brain structure whose function is beautifully organized to help ensure our survival as a species, it is the SCN. Even the SCN’s seeming imperfection turns out to be perfect after all.

Stay with me here. For example, the SCN generates a period—meaning a cycle length—that is close to but not quite twenty-four hours. The SCN’s period tends to be a bit longer than that, up to 24.5 hours. [^29] By virtue of this, it can shift the start of the circadian rhythm forward or backward according to seasonal changes in day length or other survival-based needs, without making a mess and setting our cells on different schedules. [^30] In other words, allowing a little room in its period duration affords us more flexibility and overall precision, not less, which is great because as we all know life is rarely the same from one day to the next. What’s more, it is also what allows for phase shifting, [^31] or the ability to change the start time of the daily cycle. If you’re wondering why this doesn’t have us waking up later and going to sleep later each day, it’s because viewing morning light and evening light nudges your clock back and forth perfectly, to keep it regular. Later I’ll explain how you can leverage that to overcome jet lag or any new schedule fast, but for now, all you need to know is that the not-exactly-twenty-four-hour rhythm is a feature, not a flaw.

As you probably already realize from the call to action that is Sleep Protocol 1, our SCN cares about whether it is light or dark out. And of course light-dark cycles are set by the spin of the earth. But how is it that our SCN—a tiny cluster of neurons embedded deep in the darkness of our brains—“knows” about the spin of the earth? Let’s consider how to answer that question with insights from planetary science and cosmology.

We’re all on this big sphere in space, spinning around at about one thousand miles per hour, causing us to face the sun, then away from the sun, then back toward the sun every twenty-four hours. Because the earth is round, the exact duration of sunlight we can experience each day depends, of course, on where we happen to be on earth. The variability is large, ranging from rather equal light-dark splits at the equator to nearly full days and/or nights of darkness or sunlight exposure at the poles. But no matter where we are on earth, inside each of our brains, our SCN steadily churns out that slightly longer than twenty-four-hour rhythm of coordinated cellular activity across our whole body.

Ultimately it is our SCN that tells us when to sleep and when to wake. We are a diurnal, not a nocturnal, species. We can stay up late and sleep all day if we choose, but even for night owls, all our bodily systems of hormones and neurotransmitters, our immune system, our levels of focus and quality of that focus, all of it, function much better when we live diurnally and wake just before or during the early daylight hours and go to sleep some hours after sundown. [^32] (Yes, night owls would be wise to do this too—that is, if mental and physical health are your priority.)

Keep in mind these are independent phenomena; the earth’s spin and travel around the sun is not what causes our SCN to have a twenty-four-hour rhythm, nor does it tell us when to sleep and when to wake, but they do need to be linked. So how do we link—or what is called entrain—our SCN’s rhythm with the light-dark cycle generated by the earth’s spin and travel around the sun? Remember, our SCN resides deep in our brain. It lives in the darkness of our skulls. To synchronize our circadian clock with the day-night cycle cast on us by our location on earth, we need a way for the presence or absence of sunlight to be conveyed to the SCN. And the best way to do that is to call upon the one part of our brain that has direct access to sunlight: our eyes.
Your Eyes

Wait, did I say that your eyes are part of your brain? Yes, that is correct. Lining the inside-back part of each of your eyeballs is a thin sheet of brain tissue called the neural retina. Your neural retinas were squeezed out and away from the rest of your brain during the first trimester of your life, while you were still in your mother’s womb, and then grew wirelike extensions into the brain proper, forming two optic nerves. Your optic nerves convey electrical signals about the presence or absence of sunlight, objects, faces, moving vehicles, and on and on to different brain areas, including—you guessed it—the SCN. [^33]

The connections between your eyes and your brain are truly a spectacular product of biological engineering. First, they solve the problem of how to inform image-forming regions of your brain about “what is out there” in the world, so you can see faces, moving objects, and colors. They also solve the problem of letting your SCN know “when it is out there” in the world, by the presence of sunlight. The neurons that convey the presence of sunlight to the SCN are not of the image-forming kind; they don’t respond to the shape of the sun, but instead to its brightness and to the specific wavelengths of sunlight that reach your eyes when the sun is low in the sky. We refer to these specific wavelengths as low solar angle sunlight. [^34]

Have you ever noticed that low solar angle sunlight appears more yellow than midday sun? Or even orange? Check out a sunrise or sunset and compare the color of sunlight to the color of sunlight at noon. Of course, sunlight doesn’t change according to where it is in the sky, but what portions of sunlight are visible to us does.

Sunlight is always full spectrum: It contains all wavelengths of light, red-orange-yellow-green-blue-indigo-violet, or ROYGBIV, just as they taught us in elementary school. The R(ed), O(range), and Y(ellow) are longer wavelengths of light, the G(reen) is medium wavelength, and the B(lue), I(ndigo), and V(iolet) are shorter wavelengths. And of course, the sun emits UV and far-red, or infrared wavelengths, too, but we can’t see those (although many other animals and insects can). When the sun is high in the sky, it appears white, because all the wavelengths of light arrive at our eyes at roughly the same intensities. When the sun is low in the sky, we see the sun as more yellow, orange, or red, because molecules in the atmosphere preferentially redirect the shorter blue, indigo, and violet wavelengths of light—a process called Rayleigh scattering. (We’ll discuss the properties of light in depth in chapter 5.)

All mammals, us humans included, have evolved a special system of light detection that responds specifically to the presence and contrast of short and long wavelengths of bright light, which is exactly what reaches your eyes if you view sunlight early or late in the day, while the sun is fairly low in the sky. In other words, we all have a sunrise and sunset detecting system in our eyes that communicates the time of day to our SCN. [^35]

As I mentioned earlier, this timekeeping eye-to-brain circuit is also a fairly recent discovery. And by recent, I mean recent: In the late 1990s, there still wasn’t general agreement among circadian biologists whether light—and not some other cue like social interactions—was the dominant force entraining our SCN. Then, in 1998, neuroscientist Ignacio “Iggy” Provencio made a key discovery. Iggy found a molecule in the skin of an African frog species that caused its skin to darken when exposed to sunlight was also present in the eyes of mice. [^36] The molecule was an opsin, which is a kind of protein that absorbs light, and when it does, it changes its conformation to set off a signaling cascade. [^37] Since the same opsin was known to cause darkening of dermal melanophores in frog skin, Provencio called the mouse retinal opsin melanopsin. Other labs confirmed melanopsin-containing cells are abundant in the human retina, too, mostly in the lower portion that views the upper visual field, which, you might have guessed, corresponds to the sky. [^38]

So we have a frog-skin-like set of cells in our eyes? Not quite. To explain what makes melanopsin-containing retinal cells so special, first a bit about photoreceptors. Photoreceptors are neurons that convert light into electrical signals the rest of the retina and brain can interpret. But the retinal cells that contain melanopsin are not like other photoreceptors. The melanopsin-containing retinal neurons Iggy discovered turned out to be both photoreceptive and retinal ganglion cells—the neurons that connect the eyes to the brain and the very cells whose wirelike extensions, or axons, make up the optic nerves. Soon after, a group of neuroscientists, David Berson and Felice Dunn at Brown University and Samer Hattar and King Wai-Yau at Johns Hopkins University, along with several of their students and postdocs, confirmed that melanopsin RGCs send their axons to the SCN and that they fire electric signals, thereby releasing neurotransmitters, when light is shone on them. [^39] Remarkably, they did this when they were isolated from all other retinal cells. As long as the light shone was very bright and long lasting, they fired electrical signals. These cells were therefore named intrinsically photosensitive RGCs (ipRGCs) to differentiate them from the other 99 percent of RGCs that can’t respond directly to light on their own. Some years later, work from the Neitz Color Vision Lab at the University of Washington in Seattle and by others showed that the optimal stimulus for ipRGCs isn’t just bright light. [^40] They discovered that the best way to activate the ipRGCs that connect to the SCN is with sustained very bright light, similar to what we see as blue or green light, contrasted with medium wavelengths of light, or what we typically see as yellow or orange—in other words, features prominent in low solar angle sunlight. The color contrasts in sunrises and sunsets tell your brain about what time it is in the twenty-four-hour cycle. That collection of work, from the discovery of melanopsin to ipRGCs, and how they work, was revelatory. It meant that there was a specific neural circuit extending from the eye to the brain dedicated to entraining the SCN and our circadian rhythms. That circuit is tuned to—neuroscience lingo for “responds to”—the presence of low solar angle sunlight. The SCN then handles the job of body- and brain-wide synchronization of circadian rhythmicity. This sunlight-driven circadian entrainment circuit requires no learning or practice to activate. It is present from birth and functions the first time and every time to control, among other things, your sleep-wake cycle.
The Sun

Which brings us to the final piece of the puzzle—the part that is not hard-wired but that you control with your behavior—and that is the call to action of this protocol: exposing your eyes to morning sunlight (or in its absence, to the next best alternative, which I describe below). Doing so activates the ipRGC-to-SCN circadian entrainment circuit and initiates dozens of beneficial processes that get and keep your brain and body going throughout the day. And toward the evening, it puts you in the best possible position to get a great night’s sleep.

In fact, we have copious evidence that this is foundational to both our daytime well-being and nighttime sleep. As one small example, a group of architects and neurologists came together in 2014 to investigate how windowless offices affected the people who worked in them. [^41] They asked twenty-seven office workers who had either no windows, or work areas situated far from windows, and twenty-two people working in offices with windows, about their well-being and sleep quality. The questionnaire scores were decidedly poorer among the windowless workers. They reported more sleep disturbances and an overall unsatisfactory quality of sleep.

In the early 2000s, a group of chronobiologists (scientists who study biological timing) at the Institute for Medical Psychology, in Munich, Germany, surveyed five hundred people about their sleep times, light exposure, and chronotype—as in, morning person, night owl, et cetera (you’ll find out how to determine yours in Sleep Protocol 4). [^42] They found that the amount of light exposure during the day correlated with what time people went to bed: More exposure during the day meant earlier bedtimes. This link can be partly explained by external factors, like employment: People whose livelihoods depend on being outdoors are more likely to be early-to-bed types, especially if their work requires them to rise early or is physically demanding. But that doesn’t explain the connection entirely. It turns out that it’s also due, in part, to the fact that exposure to daylight has a regulating effect on our physiology—causing elevated levels of alertness by a host of different pathways, including hormonal and neural pathways. As one review put it, “In sum, research seems to agree that daylight (at high intensities) is beneficial for sleep.” [^43]

There are also numerous studies showing that bright-light exposure early in the day—at the intensities that one would get from being outdoors in the morning—is beneficial for everything from mood to hormone health, daytime energy levels, and on and on. [^44] But before you say, “Okay, got it!,” there’s just a bit more to understand about the underlying mechanisms in this protocol, and that’s the relationship between sleep and wakefulness. And it will help you get the most out of this protocol, regardless of where you live and the time of year.

Our daytime levels of alertness reflect the quality and duration of our nighttime sleep. That’s a giant “duh.” We all know that if we sleep poorly, we drag both mentally and physically the next day. We also all know that if we sleep great, we’re focused and motivated to do all kinds of things that require energy… and that we have the energy to do them.

But what most people do not know is that the relationship between sleep and wakefulness works in the other direction too. When we are alert during the morning and daytime, we are more likely to expend mental and physical energy that in turn helps us sleep at night. Even those of us who sleep well typically find that increasing our daytime physical activity—especially in the hours between sunrise and 2:00 p.m.—leads to significantly better sleep, [^45] which in turn leads to more energy the next day, which improves sleep, and so on. Again, you’re probably thinking, “This is common knowledge. Do we really need science to explain this?”

Here is the lesser-known fact: Morning sunlight viewing is the best way to increase our morning and daytime energy levels. [^46] Not food (although fine to eat early in the day), not caffeine (also fine). It’s morning sunlight.

Morning sunlight increases your energy levels through at least three different mechanisms. First, it suppresses any residual melatonin you may have circulating in your brain (Sleep Protocol 3 includes an extensive look at melatonin, a hormone that helps promote sleepiness). [^47] As discussed above, when the ipRGCs are activated by sunlight viewing, they send electrical signals to the SCN. The SCN, in turn, stimulates a collection of neurons in the nearby paraventricular nucleus, or PVN. The PVN then sets off a cascade of signals that go through the spinal cord and back up to the pineal gland in the brain, shutting off melatonin production. [^48] Voila! You’ve suppressed the primary hormone that promotes sleepiness by viewing morning sunlight.

Second, bright light reaching your eyes helps suppress the action of adenosine, a chemical that also leads to feelings of sleepiness. [^49] Sunlight does this indirectly via its effects on other systems in the brain and body, but nonetheless, it has a potent adenosine-reducing effect. (We’ll take a deep dive into adenosine in Sleep Protocol 7). After a full night’s sleep, adenosine levels tend to be low, but if you happen to not get enough sleep (as so many of us do), morning light helps reduce any residual adenosine. That both increases your alertness and prevents the residual adenosine from delaying your circadian clock, which would otherwise bias you toward waking up later the next day, then going to sleep later, then waking up even later the following day, and so on (what chronobiologists call a phase delay). [^50] Such circadian “drift” brought on by mild sleep deprivation is very common. It is best remedied by viewing morning sunlight to reset your circadian rhythm. [^51]

Third, we need to talk about cortisol. Because it’s often discussed in the context of chronic stress, which is bad, most people think cortisol is “bad” too. But it’s not bad. Cortisol is essential to health and your levels of energy—you just don’t want your cortisol levels to be elevated at the wrong times. [^52]

Your SCN is located in your hypothalamus (H), which is part of a biological circuit that also includes your pituitary gland (P), a small, stalk-like protrusion at the base of your brain that releases hormones into your bloodstream. The circuit also includes your adrenal glands (A), which reside atop your kidneys. This circuit is known as the HPA axis. [^53] The HPA axis is one of the main systems that responds to stress (which is why you’ll hear more about it in chapter 3). Here’s how it works: It starts with signals from the hypothalamus, which then stimulate the release of specific hormones from the pituitary, which in turn stimulate adrenaline and cortisol release from your adrenals.

The HPA axis is also involved in the sleep-wake cycle. When your ipRGCs are activated by low solar angle morning sunlight and your SCN receives the ensuing signal, it alerts your adrenal glands to release adrenaline and cortisol via the HPA axis. [^54] Cortisol and adrenaline dramatically increase levels of alertness, the latter likely by activating receptors on your vagus nerve, [^55] a large portion of which extends from the organs in your body up into your brain and stimulates areas there such as the locus coeruleus to make norepinephrine, which has the net effect of “waking” you up. [^56] Cortisol does a lot of things. It also decreases inflammation and regulates our immune systems to protect against viral and bacterial infections. [^57] And it helps regulate our energy levels. Think about cortisol as a wakefulness-promoting hormone, not a stress hormone, if you want to understand what the cortisol in your body is doing most of the time. It’s also useful to consider how cortisol ebbs and flows across time due to signals from your circadian clock. By measuring cortisol levels every twenty minutes in human subjects, researchers found cortisol reaches its apex at about sixty minutes or so after you wake up and that it is lowest about four to five hours after you fall asleep. [^58] Then it begins to rise sharply across the final two to three hours of your sleep until—boom! You wake up due in large part to what is called the cortisol awakening response (CAR). Yes, reaching a threshold level of cortisol is a major factor in what ultimately rouses you from sleep. As mentioned above, your cortisol continues to rise and peaks about sixty minutes after waking, then slowly drops down as you head into the early and late afternoon. Cortisol levels generally stay low and continue to drop in the evening and at nighttime (assuming it doesn’t spike from stress or intense exercise—more on that below), and then it falls to its nadir in those first four to five hours of sleep before starting to rise again toward morning. We return to this circadian cortisol curve in chapter 3, and the role it plays in promoting health in women and men of all ages. For now, the key thing to know is that for cortisol to support our health, it needs to peak in the first hour or so after waking; it then needs to drop precipitously in the evening and night and continue falling to reach its nadir in those initial four to five hours of sleep. [^59]

Viewing morning sunlight doesn’t directly cause the morning peak in cortisol, but it can dramatically amplify its rise by as much as 50 percent. [^60] This also helps ensure that this peak comes early in the day and isn’t shifted to the afternoon. Late-day elevations in cortisol have negative consequences over time such as sleeplessness, anxiety, and metabolic disease. [^61]

A quick note: A morning workout, morning caffeine, and breakfast (provided it isn’t a huge and/or carbohydrate-laden one) will all promote wakefulness, too, and thereby contribute to a well-aligned circadian rhythm. But morning sunlight is the most potent lever for increasing morning cortisol and thus energy during your day, and for improving your sleep at night. Don’t underestimate its power.
Keep your circadian rhythm attuned to the sun, and all of these mechanisms will work as they should.
COMMON QUESTIONS
It’s often dark when I wake up. What do I do if I have no access to morning sunlight but I want to start my day

If you wake up before sunrise, and you want to start your day, I suggest turning on as many bright indoor lights in your home—or hotel room, or wherever you may be—as possible. Sunlight cannot be replaced by standard indoor lighting, but turning on indoor lighting first thing won’t hurt. Then get outside to view morning sunlight once the sun is up.

If you wake before sunrise every day, or if you live in a part of the world where it is very dark in winter, you may want to invest in a 10,000 lux light to help ensure you get enough light in the morning (lux is a measure of brightness). Most cost about $100, and some are portable for travel. I often wake up before sunrise, and because the ipRGCs can be activated by very bright artificial lights if those bright lights include sufficient short wavelengths, I keep a 10,000 lux lamp in my kitchen and bathroom. [^62] It lacks long wavelength light, so I also have a red incandescent light next to it and I turn that on too. I use the red incandescent light from SaunaSpace (no affiliation). I turn them both on first thing in the morning and then I get outside to view morning sunlight once the sun is up. I am well aware these lights are not a replacement for sunlight, but they help bridge the gap until the sun is up. Once the sun is up, you can be sure I go outside to view it!

And I will sometimes keep the 10,000 lux lamp and a red incandescent light on and facing me for an hour or so once I’m back working at my desk or getting ready for the day. Chapter 5 further explains the logic and benefits of this extended morning light exposure. There I also mention options that can be of real help for sleep as well as other aspects of health too, such as metabolic health.

But remember, morning sunlight is the best stimulus for your ipRGCs, SCN, and circadian rhythm, and it costs nothing! Figure out how to view it each morning. Again, you don’t need to see it cross the horizon as it rises. If you do, great, but if you wake up after sunrise, that’s fine. Do your best to view sunlight within the first thirty to sixty minutes after waking up. Bring your coffee or tea outside with you. Bring your spouse or kids if they’re awake. Bring your dog if you have one. Remember, dogs, cats, cows, and other animals have ipRGCs and an SCN, too, and they benefit from morning sunlight in many of the same ways and via the same mechanisms as we do. [^63]
What if it’s cloudy outside
To activate your ipRGCs fastest, go outside and face east toward the sun on a nice, clear morning with no clouds in the sky. Obviously, this isn’t possible for everyone every day.

Again, fortunately, sparse clouds do not interfere with the interaction between sunlight and our circadian clock. However, if the sky is densely overcast and gray, a 10,000 lux light can be a real help, but still aim for getting more sunlight in your eyes to compensate for the lower intensity of sunlight and reduced yellow-blue contrast exposure you’re likely to get on very overcast days. In fact, it’s especially important that you get sunlight in your eyes on overcast days. This is for three reasons: (1) dense clouds reduce the number of photons reaching your eyes in a given amount of time; (2) they filter out much of the longer (yellow, orange, and red) wavelengths of light, and (3) you are likely to be indoors more on cloudy days, which can cause the SCN to fall out of sync with the solar cycle, which leads to later nights, more artificial light exposure at night, more circadian disruption, and so on.

Aim to extend the sunny, clear day recommendation of a minimum of five to ten minutes, to at least fifteen minutes on cloudy days, and thirty minutes (minimum) on densely overcast days. That may seem like a long time, but remember, you don’t need to stand in one place gazing at the sky. Take a walk. Make a call. Listen to a book or podcast or talk to a friend, partner, or other family member. And even if you can’t be outside for the full time recommended above, some sunlight hitting your eyes in the morning is better than none. If you miss a day completely due to travel or sickness or other reasons, don’t despair—your energy levels that day may be lower because you didn’t get the cortisol spike bright morning light causes, but your circadian rhythm is the reflection of your previous three to four days of sunlight viewing activity.
Do I need to worry about sunlight damaging my eyes

Excessive UV light exposure can cause cataracts and, as we have all heard, skin damage, accelerated skin aging, and some forms of skin cancer, topics I cover in more detail later in the book. But viewing morning sunlight is much safer than viewing overhead midday sunlight—because that Rayleigh scattering of short wavelength light when the sun is low in the sky includes UV and thus reduces your UV exposure significantly. It is when the sun is overhead that the UV index is high. UV light isn’t bad, per se, but you don’t want too much of it reaching your eyes or skin. Chapter 5 goes into the benefits and drawbacks of UV.

NEVER, EVER force yourself to stare at the sun—or any light source for that matter, at any time of day. Your natural blink and “look away” reflex is a built-in circuit (yes, there is a dedicated circuit for this) to protect your eyes. People with macular degeneration or other eye conditions ought to be especially careful about viewing midday sunlight, and if very sensitive to sunlight, they may want to consult with their ophthalmologist before doing any deliberate sunlight viewing.
What about eyeglasses and contact lenses
Eyeglasses and contact lenses are both perfectly fine to wear while viewing morning sunlight. Neither one blocks light from reaching your eyes, even if your eyeglasses or contacts have UV filters.

Sunglasses and transition lenses, however, should be avoided while viewing morning sunlight because they block out a lot of the relevant wavelengths that trigger the valuable mechanisms covered in this protocol. Moreover, they reduce the number of photons reaching your eyes. Of course it’s fine to wear sunglasses as needed for comfort and safety at other times of day.
What about viewing sunlight through a window or windshield? Is that the same

People relentlessly ask me this and my response is equally persistent: No, it’s not the same. It’s far less effective, though better than nothing. But if there is any way to get outside, do. Windows and windshields, especially nowadays, filter the intensities and wavelengths you want for this protocol to work. “How come viewing morning sunlight through eyeglasses or contacts is fine but not windows or windshields?” you may wonder. Because windows do something called spectral filtering: They reduce the amount of light—especially short wavelength light—that would otherwise reach your eyes. Corrective lenses don’t; they let far more light through. That’s their job. Well, that and to correct any optical errors in the structure of your eyeballs so you can see things clearly. Windows and windshields do neither.
SLEEP PROTOCOL 2 View Sunlight in the Late Afternoon
WHAT TO DO

• Get sunlight in your eyes in the late afternoon or early evening. Ideally, go outside and spend at least ten to fifteen minutes there before the sun sets. If at all possible, face or walk west toward the sun. You do not need to see the sun drop below the horizon. That’s a wonderful thing if you can—who doesn’t love a sunset? Alas, most of us don’t live or work in the right place to do so. Luckily, just going outside and getting some ambient light in your eyes in the late afternoon or early evening is beneficial. Seeing the sunset is a bonus.

• A few things to keep in mind. As with the previous protocol, it is best to face the sun directly, not through a window or windshield, and without wearing sunglasses or a brimmed hat. Perhaps you can get an unobscured view by going up to a rooftop or by walking a few blocks from where you work or live. From a health perspective, that is well worth it. Again it’s especially important to do this protocol on overcast days.
HOW IT WORKS

We’ve already unpacked the basic physiological processes linking your circadian clock, your eyes, and specific qualities of light that drive the sleep-wake cycle. Afternoon sunlight exposure taps into some of the same basic underlying cells, circuits, and mechanisms, but has both distinct and added benefits, including partially protecting you from some of the negative health effects of viewing artificial lights late at night.

Here again we start with the SCN. Earlier I described the SCN as a “cluster of neurons,” but that doesn’t really do it justice. A key feature of the SCN is that it contains two oscillators, each following a roughly twenty-four-hour rhythm of electrical activity, but offset from one another. [^64] It’s as if they are singing in a round, with peaks happening at different yet specific moments within the twenty-four-hour cycle. One peak roughly corresponds to morning and the other to evening, and each can be entrained to sunrise and sunset. And they communicate with one another to be sure neither the morning nor the evening oscillator runs too fast or too slow. That helps generate the SCN’s coherent daily rhythm that all other cells in the body follow. It also allows us to shift our clock forward or back as the lengths of days and nights change across the seasons.

Here’s the best way to think about it: These two oscillators are like bookends buttressing a row of vertically stacked books, making the books less likely to fall over. This is the right analogy given that viewing morning sunlight shifts the phase of our circadian clock forward, making us want to go to sleep earlier and wake up earlier. Viewing late afternoon or early evening sunlight delays the phase of our clock, which, because it shifts the timing of the release of hormones like melatonin, makes us want to go to bed later and wake up later. So viewing both morning and afternoon sunlight thus helps keep us on a regular sleep-wake schedule, because the phase shift effects of morning and evening sunlight offset each other. [^65]

Another great reason to view sunlight in the late afternoon or early evening is that it helps buffer us against the negative effects of viewing bright artificial lights at night. [^66] In the morning, we need to see a lot of bright light to train our SCN with the solar cycle, and to elevate our levels of alertness. Unless it’s a 10,000 lux lamp, most artificial lights and certainly our phone or computer screens just can’t do the job at that time. After sundown, however, it takes extremely little bright light to quash our melatonin levels, and shift our circadian clock. And even if we can still fall asleep at night, that sleep is not going to be as high quality.

In fact, studies show that as little as fifteen seconds of bright light can significantly shift our circadian clock. [^67] And while most screens are not as bright as the lights used in these studies, our ipRGCs and SCN work to sum photons—that is, add up all the light we see from various sources. And let’s face it, most people are looking at their phone and other screens for a lot longer than fifteen seconds after sundown.

To recap: In the morning, you need more bright light in your eyes than a screen or conventional home lighting can provide, and at night you want far less light reaching your eyes than typically comes from a phone or computer screen or conventional home lighting. It all has to do with how our eyes are more sensitive to detecting light at different times of day or night. If that seems inconvenient, you’re right; nowadays it is! But the circuits underlying retinal and circadian sensitivity across the twenty-four-hour cycle evolved long before humans had artificial lighting, much less the bright, short-wavelength-enriched LED screens and LED bulbs that we use today.

I, like most people, often wake up once in the middle of the night to use the bathroom. If I had things my way, our circadian system would be buffered from the phase-shifting effects of light at that time, but I wasn’t consulted at the design phase, and our ipRGCs are exquisitely sensitive to bright light in the middle of the night and wee hours of morning. In fact, our ipRGCs and SCN become increasingly responsive to light with every hour after sundown. [^68] If you’re wondering if fireplaces, campfires, candlelight, or moonlight are too bright to view after dark, the answer is no. Firelight sources emit very long wavelengths, and moonlight is low lux. Candlelight is typically just 1 lux. A bright, full moon is less than 1 lux! Compare those numbers to a typical table lamp, which is 200 to 400 lux, or commonly used overhead indoor LED lighting, which is 500 to 1,000 lux.

So are we to all avoid artificial lighting and opt for candlelight or moonlight? Maybe, but more on that later. In the meantime, let’s acknowledge that most people just won’t do that, and even if we opt to at home, we can’t control the lighting of most other environments like office cubicles, restaurants, hotels, and the rest.

That is where this protocol can help. Viewing sunlight in the afternoon reduces the sensitivity of neural circuits in your retinas, so that any artificial light you see after dark does not have as strong an effect in disrupting melatonin and other circadian-related molecules and processes in your eyes and brain. This protocol is especially important if your mornings and days are mostly spent under artificial indoor lights, as that will cause any artificial lights you view at night to have an outsized negative effect on your sleep and circadian rhythms. [^69] Think of viewing the sunset as your (partial!) nighttime TV-watching or phone-scrolling inoculation. That said, you should still strive to dim the lights in the evening, and make it as dark as possible while you sleep, as discussed in the next protocol.
