HOW IT WORKS

First off, it’s important to emphasize that NSDR is not anything like traditional meditation. NSDR is not breathwork either. Rather, NSDR belongs to a category of techniques that can be broadly thought of as self-directed relaxation. NSDR is also not anything like a nap. A central feature of NSDR is to stay awake (but not focused on planning or action), while simultaneously bringing the body into an extremely relaxed state. It puts you in a unique brain state. [^172] Meditation often involves holding one’s attention on a specific location inside or near one’s body (such as the spot just behind our forehead), or on an external object (a candle flame, for example), or even on a sensory experience (e.g., the taste of a single almond). These kinds of directed perceptual focus exercises have been shown to improve concentration, reduce stress, strengthen memory and improve mental health. [^173] When done consistently, meditation techniques can lead to profound shifts in our awareness of our internal thought patterns. And over time, meditation can provide a rich understanding of how our minds work and can even change our temperament.

Self-directed relaxation protocols like NSDR are different. NSDR involves shifting our autonomic nervous system into a more parasympathetic, or relaxed, state by breathing in a manner in which the duration of our exhales is deliberately emphasized. [^174] NSDR also involves deliberately and systematically moving our focus of attention from one part of our body to another, then to locations far from our body, then closer to us, then away again. The focusing, then defocusing, and moving and resetting of attention over and over keeps the mind active. And because it is done while the body is deeply relaxed, it brings about a somewhat dreamlike state, and yet you are completely aware and alert.

NSDR is a modification of an ancient practice known as yoga nidra, which roughly translates to “yoga sleep.” [^175] Yoga nidra has been described as creating the experience of moving our mind away “from thinking and doing toward a state of being and feeling”—which is an admittedly vague statement. There is a small but growing body of modern science on the brain and bodily states that yoga nidra and NSDR bring about and their ability to restore mental and physical vigor, improve consolidation of newly learned information, offset sleep loss, and more.

When I first tried yoga nidra in 2017, I found it to be incredibly restorative. Doing this technique for twenty to thirty minutes first thing in the morning after a restless or less-than-full night’s sleep left me feeling fully rested, like I’d had the best sleep of my life. I also noticed that incorporating this practice in the morning improved my ability to fall back asleep quickly if I happened to wake up in the middle of the night. That’s right—even though NSDR stands for non-sleep deep rest, and even though it is typically done in the morning or afternoon, something about doing it at that time significantly improved my ability to self-direct my brain and body into a relaxed state and drift back to sleep at night if ever I needed to. What’s more, if I ever woke up in the middle of the night, listening to a guided NSDR recording beat tossing and turning, and often sent me back to sleep. Challenges with falling asleep and staying asleep are very common, so I was intrigued. I also noticed that replacing an afternoon nap with an NSDR session left me feeling especially reinvigorated and did not alter my nighttime sleep in any negative way.

I wondered how this simple practice really worked. So I dove into the literature and found there wasn’t much known. But the few studies I did find were interesting. A 2002 study from Denmark found that doing yoga nidra dramatically increases levels of dopamine in a brain region called the basal ganglia, which are involved in taking, and withholding, action. [^176] Yoga nidra also reduced people’s blood pressure and heart rate. Although this and other studies of yoga nidra were small in terms of the number of subjects studied, other investigations indicated that this practice could improve various measures of mental health and help consolidate certain forms of learning. [^177]

At one point, I decided to devote a portion of my lab to studying yoga nidra as a tool for stress reduction. To do so we needed to keep its core elements—breathing that emphasizes long exhales to slow the heart rate and place us into a more parasympathetic state, the deliberate and systematic movement of one’s perceptual attention to the surface and then the interior of the body, then away from the body, and so on—but we opted to remove the “intentions” and any language pertaining to more spiritual aspects of yoga nidra. [^178] This parsing was not an attempt at cultural appropriation of an ancient tradition. Rather, it was a way to examine this powerful tool within the context of Western science, where we seek to understand what works and why, and to then use this knowledge to build more efficient and effective tools. Any aspect of the practice that couldn’t be reliably measured was discarded.

Later, as I moved into public education and spoke about stress mitigation tools, I coined the term non-sleep deep rest, which keeps the key elements related to the physiology of yoga nidra, but removes the subjective aspects that are hard to keep constant from one person to the next.

And eventually, given the wide interest in stress mitigation tools, my podcast team produced various NSDR scripts of short (ten minute), medium (twenty minute), and long (thirty minute) durations and made them freely available online. [^179]

Public feedback has confirmed the positive effects of NSDR, but of course it just follows the thousands of years of people across the world doing this time-tested practice. (Later in chapter 3, I’ll get back to what my lab’s studies on stress discovered about the benefits of NSDR).

Among all the protocols that I have shared on the Huberman Lab podcast, NSDR is in the top ten of those that people tell me have changed their lives, especially individuals who struggle to sleep enough, to maintain high levels of daytime energy and focus, and also among those struggling with excessive work, school, or other demands. I am the last person in the world to suggest people sleep less than they need to at night, but I will be the first to acknowledge how challenging it can often be to get a full seven to nine hours of sleep, especially for parents of young children and those working very long hours. NSDR is a remarkable tool for anyone who simply can’t get enough sleep because they have to wake up and meet the demands of the day. Or for those who don’t like naps or who can’t nap for whatever reason. We will revisit NSDR several times in this book, but in the meantime, if you’re seeking tools for improving sleep, or even replacing missed sleep, I highly suggest doing NSDR.
COMMON QUESTIONS
What if I fall asleep during NSDR

That’s just fine. Chances are, if done during the daytime, the sleep will be relatively shallow and won’t create much, if any, sleep inertia. On many occasions, I have fallen asleep during a morning or afternoon NSDR session and then woken up at the last instruction to move my limbs, which meant I wasn’t in a deep sleep. If you are using NSDR to reset during the day, or first thing in the morning to offset the effects of not getting enough sleep, just be sure you set an alarm in case you fall asleep.
How long should my NSDR session be

That’s up to you. A ten-minute NSDR is often enough for a quick afternoon reset, but I suggest doing a twenty- to thirty-minute NSDR if you have time. If you slept poorly the night before, you may find that a longer session in the morning or afternoon leaves you feeling more rested, compensating for the sleep you missed in the night. Find what works for you.
Can NSDR truly replace sleep or reduce the amount of time I need to sleep

Claims that “thirty minutes of yoga nidra is worth two hours of sleep” abound. I’ve also heard that “twenty minutes of meditation twice daily reduces your nighttime sleep needs by several hours.” I am not aware of much laboratory data supporting those statements. It can be hard to get enough sleep, and most of us would love to need less of it to feel fully rested. NSDR won’t necessarily reduce the amount of nighttime sleep you need, but it may very well improve the quality of the sleep you get. Combined with proper placement of your nighttime sleep in the twenty-four-hour cycle (see Sleep Protocol 4 for more), and other protocols in this chapter, it may, however, reduce your total sleep needs by improving your sleep architecture, as we discussed earlier in this chapter.

In one study, researchers randomized forty-one people with chronic insomnia to participate in either cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia or twice-daily yoga nidra for twenty minutes per session. [^180] In both groups, participants slept a few minutes longer during the study than at the start of it. However, the yoga nidra group fell asleep faster, fell back asleep faster after night wakings, and had a more efficient sleep (an increase in the number of times they went through N1, N2, N3, and REM) compared to their sleep prior to the study. So while they weren’t sleeping less, the sleep they were getting was better than before.

The study also found a significant reduction in cortisol following yoga nidra. [^181] That may be one factor that reduces the total amount of sleep you need because, in theory, lowering your evening cortisol should improve sleep. If you practice relaxation techniques during the day and happen to need less sleep that night, that’s an added bonus. [^182]
SLEEP PROTOCOL 9 Consider Supplements to Support Sleep
WHAT TO DO

• Find a combination of supplements that support you in getting the best possible sleep. Learn a bit about how each of these works. Consider your specific needs and consult with your physician to ensure that any supplements you take are safe for you and will not interfere with any medications you are currently taking. As stated in the introduction, supplements can have their place but ideally, try behavioral tools first. There is simply no pill to replace poor sleep habits, or “sleep hygiene.” Below is a list of common supplements sold over the counter that can assist in getting the best possible night’s sleep: Magnesium L-threonate or magnesium bisglycinate.Dosage: 145–250 mg These two forms of magnesium are interchangeable for improving sleep.
• Apigenin, a derivative of chamomile. Dosage: 50 mg
• Theanine. Dosage: 100–200 mg

Start with the lowest amount listed and adjust the dosage if necessary until you find the lowest dose that works for you. The dosages provided here are averages. All the compounds are considered safe for healthy individuals but results vary, so I suggest taking one at a time for a few nights each and then adding an additional supplement. That will be the most cost-effective and safest approach, and it will help you understand what works for you. Th/at said, if you want to start with a small stack of two to three sleep supplements right out of the gate, here is one that has worked for a lot of people. Take it about thirty minutes before going to sleep. 145–250 mg magnesium L-threonate (or magnesium bisglycinate)

• Pay attention to potential side effects. The supplements listed above are generally very safe but not all of them will sit well for all people. Here’s what to watch for: Gut discomfort: A small percentage of people (about 5 percent in my experience) who take magnesium threonate as a sleep aid experience digestive issues or other gut discomfort. And always check that any product you decide to use is reliable.
HOW IT WORKS

When it comes to getting optimal sleep, it’s always best to start with behavioral tools and changes to your sleep environment. (Sun)light exposure, adjusting your core body temperature, and NSDR can all be employed to improve sleep. So, too, can exercise and proper nutrition (more on both later). These carry no cost, cause no side effects, and quite often resolve persistent issues.

Many people turn to supplements to help improve their sleep. Parsing the scientific literature on the efficacy of over-the-counter, supplement-based sleep aids can be difficult. The studies are often small, they have conflicting results, and they are too few to provide a significant body of evidence. [^183] That being said, enough data exist to indicate that some supplements may be beneficial and carry a very low risk of harm for most people trying them. In my opinion, these are much safer than the majority of prescription sleep medications.

A major issue when it comes to supplements is that the dose of the pills inside the bottle often does not match the dosage stated on the label. [^184] In addition, just because a supplement contains a “natural” ingredient does not mean it is safe. And these ingredients may react badly with a prescribed medication. So a reminder here, again, to talk to your doctor before proceeding, and to only buy supplements from reputable brands. I discuss a few things to look for on the packaging to ensure this below.

• Magnesium L-threonate: Increasing brain magnesium with this compound may improve learning and memory. [^185] A randomized study of magnesium L-threonate versus placebo found that this supplement improved the quality of sleep and also cognitive performance during the day. [^186] There are more data on magnesium bisglycinate than threonate for sleep but these seem to work interchangeably for this purpose.

• Apigenin: This compound is among the most widely studied flavonoids (chemicals found in plants) and is present in chamomile, parsley, oranges, celery, and thyme, among herbs and vegetables. [^187] A growing body of evidence supports apigenin as a sleep aid. [^188] Animal studies have found a mild sedative effect from apigenin. [^189] Studies in humans also indicate a sleep benefit. In one investigation, apigenin mildly improved daytime function among people with insomnia. [^190] Among a group of new mothers suffering from poor sleep and depression, apigenin was found to improve both.
• Theanine: Evidence suggests that theanine increases levels of GABA, an amino acid that, when broadly increased in the brain, may reduce anxiety. [^191]
• Glycine: Research suggests glycine works by elevating serotonin, which helps regulate sleep, and activating NMDA receptors in the SCN, where the circadian clock is headquartered. [^192]
• GABA: As noted earlier, GABA is an amino acid associated with reducing brain activity. It promotes relaxation and is therefore conducive to sleep. [^193]

• Melatonin: As discussed in Sleep Protocol 3, we produce natural melatonin, a hormone that causes us to feel sleepy. This production surges at night, leading to feelings of sleepiness. This hormone works well all on its own. However, melatonin supplements have been a staple of vitamin stores for years. Clinical trials and meta-analyses of multiple studies indicate that melatonin supplements may benefit older adults, who experience a lower level of natural melatonin production. [^194] It may also be beneficial in combination with morning light exposure for people with Alzheimer’s disease, [^195] which tends to disrupt sleep patterns. However, there is no clear evidence of benefit for all other populations. Once again, be aware of the dosages listed here. The amount of melatonin contained in the typical single, over-the-counter pill is far greater than what our bodies produce. I often see dosages of 3 milligrams, 5 milligrams, or even 8 to 10 milligrams of melatonin, which are incredibly high and not advised. That’s a problem, because melatonin does more than make us sleepy; it can also interact with other hormones and biological pathways in the brain and body unrelated to sleep. Therefore, taking melatonin chronically can be problematic, especially in children and adolescents who are still growing. If you decide to take melatonin, make sure that you are choosing a reputable brand with third-party certification and use the minimal effective dose. I would suggest taking no more than the amounts listed above (0.5–1.5 mg of rapid or sustained release, although it’s fine, and useful, to take both).

• Tart cherry extract: A small, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study found elevated natural melatonin levels and improved sleep quality among ten people who drank tart cherry juice for seven days. [^196] This preliminary evidence suggests a potential benefit, with larger and longer-term studies needed. Tart cherry juice is safe to try as a sleep aid taken shortly before bedtime. Tart cherry extract capsules are preferable if you don’t want the added calories from the juice.

• Kiwi extract: A small study of twenty-five people who self-reported their sleep patterns concluded that kiwi may modestly improve sleep duration and efficiency. [^197] Consuming kiwi fruit with the skin on an hour before bed may be a mild sleep aid. More evidence is needed to be certain of this benefit, but kiwi is safe to try. Kiwi extract is a good noncaloric, capsule-based approach to get the same effect. (And you don’t have to eat kiwi skins!)

It’s best to take any sleep aid supplements about thirty minutes before you intend to be asleep. Magnesium supplementation during the daytime can be useful for other reasons, but if you’re taking it specifically for sleep, best to take it before bed. The one exception is theanine, which some people like to take when they drink caffeine, in order to offset the jitters that they experience from caffeine. In fact, that is one reason energy drink manufacturers often include theanine in energy drinks.

What brand of supplements should I use

SLEEP PROTOCOL 10 Approach Prescription Sleep Drugs with Caution
WHAT TO DO

• Talk to your doctor. If you’re still struggling with sleep after working through the prior sleep protocols, and you have tried the stress-management protocols, too, talk to your doctor. There may be an underlying health condition that needs addressing. Or it may be that your sleep issues warrant more intensive treatment. Cognitive behavioral therapy has shown efficacy for sustained sleep disturbance.

• Stay away from prescription sleep aids if you can. These are best avoided, unless your physician prescribes them as a last resort. Most can carry side effects, like confusion and daytime drowsiness. Some, like Ambien, may harm sleep architecture and glymphatic function. [^199] That means even if you have more time in bed, sleep might not be doing the “cleaning” job it’s designed to do. Some, like trazodone, and the DORAs (dual orexin receptor antagonists), appear safer than the others, yet it is easy to become dependent on them for sleep once you begin. None are without side effects, and withdrawal then carries its own set of side effects.
HOW IT WORKS
Below I’ve described the different and more common classes of sleep aids, so you can understand how each works, as well as the potential risks:

• Benzodiazepines: These drugs belong to a class often referred to as hypnotics or sedatives, although they have other effects too. They are often prescribed to treat insomnia. They work by increasing the effects of GABA. [^200] They are older medications that can be addictive, and can have other serious side effects including confusion, memory problems, unsteadiness, and slurred speech. [^201] The withdrawal from benzodiazepines is notoriously hard.

• Non-benzodiazepine hypnotics: These short-term insomnia medications tend to be less disruptive than benzodiazepines. [^202] The most well-known is Ambien. However, the FDA has issued a “black box” warning for non-benzodiazepines following reports of rare but dangerous behavior during sleep, including wandering, driving, and using a stove, and amnesia and other forms of memory alterations after the drug has worn off. [^203] And again, Ambien may harm sleep architecture and glymphatic function, the clearance of waste products from the brain at night. [^204]

• Antidepressants: Drowsiness is a common side effect of certain antidepressants, leading to their use as a sleep aid. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine has recommended the use of certain antidepressants as a treatment for insomnia among people with depression, but clinical evidence for this benefit is limited. [^205] Trazodone, a serotonin receptor agonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI) seems to preserve sleep architecture better than other antidepressants when taken specifically for sleep. [^206] Please note that many people who take selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like Prozac, SARIs like trazodone, or norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitors (NDRIs) like Wellbutrin/bupropion during the daytime for depression, anxiety, or other reasons do not experience altered sleep, and some of these, like bupropion, when taken early in the daytime, can indirectly improve sleep later that night. [^207] Psychiatrists now will prescribe antidepressants specifically for sleep because some can improve sleep.

• Melatonin receptor agonists: This category of medications mimics the action of melatonin and may help with falling asleep faster and improving sleep quality. They do not appear to cause dependency or serious side effects. [^208] However, the efficacy of melatonin receptor agonists is somewhat unclear.

• Anticonvulsants and dopamine agonist drugs: These may be prescribed to treat restless legs syndrome and other conditions involving nighttime limb movement that can make it difficult to fall and stay asleep, [^209] as well as to treat pain. Examples include gabapentin and cabergoline.

• Dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs): Insomnia is characterized by abnormal wakefulness, and orexin, a neuropeptide that helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle and that is altered in narcolepsy, has been found to cause a state of arousal. [^210] Thus it makes sense to investigate orexin as a potential target for insomnia drugs. That led to the development of the DORAs, which work by reducing the action of orexin and thus wakefulness circuits in the brain rather than by direct sedation. [^211] Early evidence of such drugs shows that they do effectively block orexin, and indicate a potential role for them in safely treating insomnia. [^212] A meta-analysis of ten randomized clinical trials that combined a sample of 7,086 individuals with insomnia found these drugs to be generally safe, with a comparably lower incidence of mild side effects and with improved sleep compared to a placebo. [^213] These new medications are expensive, typically costing about $300 or more per month. [^214] Generic lower-cost versions are not yet available.
SLEEP PROTOCOL 11 Adjust Your Caffeine Schedule to Improve Your Sleep
WHAT TO DO

• Avoid caffeine in the eight to ten hours before bed. As it’s a stimulant with a long half-life, caffeine should be avoided late in the day, especially if you have trouble falling asleep. Some people who are especially caffeine sensitive may have to avoid caffeine in the twelve hours before bedtime. Even those who can “fall asleep after drinking coffee” are likely not getting the best sleep they could. As someone who loves caffeine, I relate to anyone reluctant to stop drinking caffeine in the afternoon. As painful as it can be, I personally avoid it after 2:00 p.m. most days.

• If you tend to experience an energy crash in the afternoon despite sleeping well, consider delaying drinking caffeine until thirty to ninety minutes after waking up. This slight adjustment to your caffeine schedule may help you have more sustained energy levels throughout the day and may help you avoid the need to drink caffeine after 2:00 p.m.
HOW IT WORKS

Remember adenosine, from Sleep Protocol 7? It’s a chemical that builds up in our brains as we go throughout our day, eventually making us want to sleep through a process called homeostatic sleep drive. [^215]

Our scientific understanding of adenosine is deeply intertwined with that of caffeine. [^216] The research history dates back to 1911, when Coca-Cola asked a psychologist named Harry Levi Hollingworth to investigate the effects of caffeine on human behavior because the US government was suing the company for including what it considered to be a drug with a “poisonous tendency” in the soda. (The cocaine that had once been a major ingredient of Coca-Cola had been removed years earlier.) [^217] The company wanted reliable evidence on exactly how caffeine altered human behavior. Hollingworth agreed as long as the company did not include his study results in its advertisements. He also insisted that the results be published regardless of what they revealed.

Hollingworth’s investigation is often cited as the first time that the double-blind, placebo-controlled study design entered psychological research. [^218] Although some may argue whether it was indeed a double-blind study, it is considered a landmark for its introduction of rigor into the process, and for its findings. Sixteen participants consumed caffeine daily at a range of doses (at amounts reflecting drinking a daily soda) or a placebo. They then completed various tasks that examined their alertness, coordination, and other mental skills. Caffeine undeniably improved their capacity in all these domains. The findings were favorable toward Coca-Cola because the chemical in question seemed to only help people, not hurt them, at least in the context of what was measured. But Coca-Cola wasn’t interested in sleep. (If you were wondering, the US government’s case was dismissed on a technicality when the company argued that caffeine wasn’t added to the beverage but rather was naturally occurring.)

According to Hollingworth’s report, published in the American Journal of Psychology in 1912, a few grains of caffeine taken on successive days were enough to impair sleep. [^219] The connection relied on self-reporting and each individual recording their impression about the quality of their sleep following each study day. But the findings were consistent.

Decades later we know how that happens: Caffeine leads to longer sleep latency (that is, the time it takes to fall asleep) and more nighttime waking, thus leading to reduced wakefulness the next day. [^220] We also now know that caffeine can alter sleep architecture, including less time spent in REM. [^221]

Hollingworth’s study was the first of many to come. Today we understand a great deal about how caffeine stimulates brain activity. It’s a psychoactive stimulant that increases the actions of epinephrine and dopamine, in part by increasing the availability of dopamine receptors, the sites on cells where it can attach and thereby initiate its effects. [^222] Caffeine also increases the activity of certain neural circuits and brain areas associated with alertness, such as the locus coeruleus, which we discussed earlier in this chapter. [^223] We also understand now how it interferes with sleep. That brings us back to adenosine.

Caffeine is what is called an adenosine antagonist. [^224] It parks in adenosine receptors, which prevents adenosine from exerting its normal fatigue-inducing activity in the brain. As sleep expert Matthew Walker describes it, “Caffeine keeps pulling out the chairs from under adenosine.” [^225] So even though adenosine is building up with each hour we are awake and increasingly so when we are very alert or active, our brains don’t register that fatigue or the number of hours we’ve been awake accurately. [^226] Caffeine dampens the communication between adenosine and the brain.

This process explains the phenomenon many of us know of as the caffeine crash. Once caffeine’s actions on those receptors wear off, which our metabolism accomplishes in a few hours, the non-receptor-bound adenosine that has accumulated suddenly can bind and fatigue hits us. In addition, caffeine makes our brain more active and increases our capacity for physical effort, and that generates more adenosine as a by-product, which in turn means the crash is harder than it would be without caffeine.

This all sounds rough, but I want to reiterate: I love caffeine and I have no plans to give it up. The data say caffeine in moderation is fine… and may even be good for us. A recent large-scale study involving over 100,000 subjects found that daily intake of approximately two to three cups of caffeinated coffee or tea can reduce risks of stroke and dementia. [^227]

“What is moderation?” you may be wondering. One or two cups of strong coffee, a few twelve-ounce diet sodas (we can debate artificial sweeteners later, in chapter 4, but we should all probably avoid the sugar in regular soda), or my favorite source of caffeine: hot brewed or cold brew yerba maté, which will deliver 100 to 300 milligrams of caffeine depending on the source.

The ramifications of caffeine on sleep depend on the dose of caffeine and the time of day you consume it. The closer to your to-sleep time you drink a caffeinated beverage, and the more sensitive you are to caffeine, the greater the impact it will have on sleep.

So now you may be wondering: How close is too close to your to-sleep time? This may seem somewhat obvious but most people don’t realize just how long the effects of caffeine last, and that’s what I hope to help with in this protocol.

People who are very caffeine sensitive have probably already learned by experience not to drink caffeine past a certain time of day if they hope to sleep later that night. For the rest of us who enjoy caffeine in both the morning and in the afternoon—yes, there are many of us—a bit more understanding of caffeine’s effects can go a long way toward consuming it while still experiencing great sleep.

Caffeine is hard to study. Would-be study participants who consume caffeine daily (and that includes about 85 percent of American adults, for example) would need to quit prior to joining a well-controlled investigation of the effects of caffeine, and many people just won’t abstain, even for a short while, just to be in a study. Also, researchers don’t always know when a person who is in caffeine withdrawal is back to a baseline state of sleep. [^228] And, as I’ve mentioned, people’s sensitivity to caffeine varies. [^229] That being said, the evidence shows that our sleep patterns tend to adapt to a daily dose of caffeine. Regular caffeine consumers are able to fall asleep, stay asleep, and cycle through the stages of sleep. [^230] It appears that chronic caffeine users develop a sort of sleep-tolerance for the stimulant. This is good and bad. Good, because it means folks like me can enjoy a morning yerba maté and a 2:00 p.m. espresso and still fall asleep easily at 10:00 p.m. Bad, because there is a chance that anyone drinking caffeine past noon is getting less than optimal sleep. Not everything in life is about getting the best possible sleep of course, but if you are struggling to feel rested enough in the daytime or are waking after seven to eight hours of sleep and still not feeling alert, you may try avoiding caffeine in the eight to ten or even twelve hours prior to sleep. Note how you feel. Those tracking their sleep with Eight Sleep, WHOOP, Oura rings, or other devices can see how this impacts their REM and non-REM sleep.

The recommendation to delay caffeine by sixty to ninety minutes after waking is just a suggestion. Indeed, this suggestion—when I first made it on the internet—made a lot of people VERY upset. (People don’t like it when you try to take away their morning coffee). To be clear: You don’t have to do it.

It is also not supported by a clinical trial. It is, however, supported by ample mechanistic evidence of how caffeine adjusts adenosine, and how adenosine continually reduces in the first one to two hours of the day if we don’t ingest caffeine. If you are someone who tends to experience energy crashes in the afternoon and you rely on caffeine to overcome them, I suggest at least trying to delay your morning caffeine by sixty to ninety minutes for a few days. It can be a bit painful at first, so maybe start with a thirty-minute delay, then sixty minutes, then ninety minutes, and see if you still need the afternoon caffeine kick. Then try NSDR, as described in Sleep Protocol 8, if you’re having trouble making it through the afternoon without it.

One key thing: If you like to exercise soon after you wake up and need caffeine to do so—as I and many others do—then by all means, drink it upon waking and do your workout. Just be sure to hydrate well too. Caffeine can be a mild diuretic. It’s much less of a diuretic than once thought but we tend to wake up slightly dehydrated as it is. [^231] Before you slam back two coffees, it’s probably best to hydrate first thing.
In My Experience

For my first caffeine of the day, I usually drink yerba maté, a Paraguayan (and Uruguayan and Argentine) tea that is traditionally sipped from a small gourd through a metal straw but that can also be brewed and consumed like any other tea. I’ll drink it hot or a cold-brewed canned version. Mateina is my favorite. (Note: I am a partial owner of Mateina, but I love it without bias. Also, it is a good idea to avoid drinking smoked varieties of yerba. Mateina is air-dried, not smoked.) I find that the alertness effect from yerba maté is more gradual and causes fewer jitters, and results in a milder, if any, “crash” as it wears off. Sometimes I have coffee or espresso later in the morning. My absolute favorite time for coffee is in the early afternoon, after a twenty-to-thirty-minute NSDR session. Talk about a reset. My best work sessions seem to follow this protocol. However, my sleep suffers if I drink coffee after about 3:00 p.m. I can fall asleep perfectly fine, but my sleep is not as deep (I use a sleep tracker, and it confirms that I get much less REM sleep after late-day caffeine). So I try to limit coffee and other sources of caffeine after 3:00 p.m. That’s not a hard-and-fast rule; sometimes I drink coffee late in the day, but that’s rare and I always regret it when I’m still awake at midnight.

I like to exercise first thing in the morning, within an hour or two of waking up, so on workout days my target regimen is to drink water and caffeine soon after waking, view sunlight, and then exercise. On days when I cannot exercise early, I tend to delay caffeine intake until midmorning, which I find keeps my energy levels steadier into and throughout the afternoon. On these days, I often skip afternoon caffeine because I don’t need it.
COMMON QUESTIONS
Does the source of caffeine matter

No. Different drinks contain different amounts of caffeine, and chocolate has small amounts too. [^232] But the caffeine molecule works pretty much the same regardless of where it comes from. Some drinks like yerba maté and guayusa tea also contain non-caffeine stimulants in them like theobromine—a plant alkaloid also with antioxidant properties. And of course nowadays there are hundreds of different energy drinks available that combine caffeine, neuromodulator precursors like L-tyrosine (the amino acid from which dopamine is made), taurine, and on and on. I will drink a zero-sugar energy drink now and again. I discuss these and other stimulants more in chapter 6.
Is caffeine unhealthy

Studies have consistently shown a health benefit from coffee, particularly when consumed before noon, up to a certain amount. [^233] Generally, beyond four cups per day of coffee, or the equivalent of 400 milligrams, there are diminishing returns or possibly negative consequences, although larger individuals may be able to handle more than that with no problem. [^234] Many of the benefits from coffee and tea are not from caffeine but from antioxidants contained in coffee beans and certain teas. That finding is supported by the fact that decaffeinated coffee confers the same benefit as caffeinated coffee, which includes a potential reduction in the risk of heart disease, prostate cancer, melanoma, endometrial cancer, liver conditions, type 2 diabetes, and neurodegenerative diseases. [^235] In the case of yerba maté, research suggests that it may facilitate weight loss by reducing appetite and perhaps by its effects on digestion as well as the microbiome, a critical aspect of health we will address in chapter 4. [^236]
SLEEP PROTOCOL 12 Avoid Alcohol Within Eight Hours Before Sleep
WHAT NOT TO DO

• Alcohol should not be used as a sleep aid. Alcohol severely disrupts the elegantly sequential architecture of sleep, and reduces both the total amount of deep sleep and REM sleep, so even if it helps you drift off and you sleep for seven to eight hours, it will negatively affect the quality of your sleep.
• If you drink, avoid alcohol within eight hours of the time you plan to be asleep. This timing reduces the amount of alcohol in your body by the time you go to bed.

The “What Alcohol Does to Your Body, Brain & Health” episode of the Huberman Lab podcast remains one of the top downloaded and shared podcast episodes of all time, across all podcasts. It makes clear that the data show zero to two drinks per week is fine for nonalcoholic adults without confounding medical issues. However, zero is better than any, and there is growing data on the increased risk of cancer associated with alcohol consumption. [^237]

I am not anti-alcohol! I know some people enjoy a drink now and again and that is my motivation for the inclusion of this protocol. I subscribe to a “do as you like, but know what you’re doing” philosophy. I personally don’t drink but I have never liked the taste or effects of alcohol.

But there’s a key question for everyone that has not been addressed: Are many of the negative effects of alcohol the consequence of the negative effects of alcohol on sleep? This has not been systematically studied, but for those that like a drink now and again (and also for those who abstain), keep that question in the back of your mind as you read the section below.
HOW IT WORKS

Alcohol is a sedative that affects the neural pathways associated with sleep in multiple ways. Alcohol decreases the amount of time it takes us to fall asleep. [^238] But what happens next is not good. During the first half of the night, the presence of alcohol in the body suppresses REM sleep and it takes longer for us to reach whatever REM sleep we do manage to achieve. [^239] Remember that each sleep stage is like a gate to the next, so the reduced REM means less deep sleep, and less REM in the next cycle. As discussed earlier in this chapter, REM sleep is critical to our cognitive functioning, to consolidating new information, and to daytime emotional regulation. So missing out on any amount of REM is a problem. And alcohol is a potent REM suppressor.

Alcohol has also been found to decrease the amount of growth hormone and testosterone released during the night—hormones critical for vitality and metabolism for both men and women. [^240] Normally, growth hormone is released relatively soon after falling asleep, and testosterone is released before and during REM sleep. [^241] The negative effects of alcohol on REM and these hormones happen acutely, meaning after even just a single night of drinking or for those who are alcohol sensitive, even one drink. Only if we metabolize the alcohol prior to bedtime do we avoid some of these consequences, which is why this protocol recommends a specific timing.

Chronic drinking is even more problematic for sleep. Insomnia and alcohol dependency frequently coexist, for example. [^242] The cycle is self-perpetuating in that poor sleep leads to increased caffeine and other stimulant use during the day and into the afternoon and evening, which leads to difficulty sleeping at night, which leads to alcohol intake as a sleep aid. Beyond the changes one or two drinks can make on REM sleep, people with alcohol dependency tend to have decreased amounts of both N2 and N3 sleep, the non-REM period when we sink into a deep sleep. [^243] These alterations in sleep architecture can persist for some time even after a person stops drinking. Frequent drinking also interferes with our circadian rhythm, disrupting or even decreasing the amount of melatonin our brains produce. [^244]

Adolescents are at particular risk of turning to alcohol intake as a sleep aid. In 2008, public health researchers at the University of Texas Health Science Center reported their findings from a large, yearlong study of insomnia among youth between the ages of eleven and seventeen years. They collected data on 3,134 people in this age range from a baseline date and then twelve months later and found that chronic insomnia heightened the risk of alcohol use. [^245] That’s concerning because insomnia is the most common sleep disorder among young people, and because nighttime phone use, which is very common in this age group, also interferes with sleep quality and duration. [^246] Phone use at night has been linked to insomnia. [^247]
That means there are two major risks to this age group when it comes to good sleep, not to mention the chronic stress that kids at that age face. We’ll discuss phone use in Sleep Protocol 14.
COMMON QUESTIONS
It’s not practical to avoid alcohol within eight hours of sleep because any drinking I do happens at night. How can I compensate for the negative effects of consuming alcohol close to bedtime

For most people, social drinking happens well within eight hours of going to sleep. What’s important here is that drinking this way every night, multiple times per week, or even once per week will disrupt sleep, and thereby health, in detrimental ways. Occasional alcohol use closer to bedtime, say once a month or less, is very unlikely to cause long-term problems, unless it’s excessive during that once-a-month night out.

If you drink in the eight hours before sleep, make sure you also consume sufficient water before going to sleep and after waking. Take electrolytes too if you can, and emphasize other behaviors that support great sleep, as well as a healthy microbiome, to try to offset the effects of alcohol.

To be clear, it’s good to enjoy life. If having a few drinks during a celebration or a night out now and again is how you do, you’re not alone. The important considerations are that this isn’t happening too often, that you’re not driving, that you’re not experiencing any kind of dependency, and that you’re not too young to drink (the negative effects of alcohol are much worse for the developing brain compared to the adult brain). [^248]
Does the type of alcohol matter

Not with respect to the negative effects on sleep and the microbiome. As mentioned above, no alcohol is better than any alcohol. Although many studies have been done on the potential benefits of red wine, conclusive evidence of this link does not exist. [^249] The amount of red wine you would need to drink to get benefits from grape skin, for example, would require consumption of enough alcohol to far outweigh any benefits. Put simply, the interaction between alcohol and our sleep processes is the same regardless of the drink.
SLEEP PROTOCOL 13 Avoid Cannabis as a Sleep Aid
WHAT TO DO
• Do not use cannabis specifically for sleep. Cannabis should not be used to facilitate falling asleep or returning to sleep after night wakings. It potently reduces REM sleep.

• Understand CBD’s impact on sleep. Some evidence exists on the benefit of CBD for sleep but those effects are mainly due to the reduced anxiety it causes. [^250] At higher dosages (e.g., 160 mg or more), CBD is more of a sedative. The dosage of CBD that makes it an effective sleep aid varies depending on weight and other factors. [^251]
HOW IT WORKS

Cannabis is a psychoactive drug that comes from the cannabis plant. The main chemical behind its psychoactive effects is THC (delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol). [^252] CBD, or cannabidiol, is another well-known component of the cannabis plant; this chemical technically is psychoactive, too, because it impacts the brain, but it’s not responsible for the “high” that people are usually seeking when they use cannabis. THC can impair cognitive or behavioral functioning; CBD doesn’t appear to do so. [^253] When present with THC in the cannabis plant or in an edible, CBD can modify the way that THC works in the brain, so their ratios can determine the subjective effects of the drug. [^254]

THC potently reduces the amount of REM sleep even at low doses. [^255] THC is often used as an aid for falling asleep, as its psychoactive properties are often accompanied by, or followed by, drowsiness. As with alcohol, people often come to depend on THC to fall asleep, which disrupts the sleep-wake cycle, and can put them at risk for the physical and mental health issues associated with a deficiency in REM sleep, including depression and cardiovascular disease, among other issues. [^256] Not everyone who uses cannabis experiences these challenges of course but the link between REM sleep and health is solid: THC reduces REM. Ask people who have used cannabis regularly and then stopped and you’ll often hear about the wild dreams they experience afterward. That is the REM-rebound compensation for the lack of REM they experienced while using cannabis. [^257]

A multidisciplinary team at McMaster University, in Canada, conducted a review of the scientific literature on the link between cannabinoids and sleep. [^258] One of their most noteworthy findings was that the direct effects of both THC and CBD on sleep are lacking data because most clinical studies of cannabis have focused on various health conditions, such as pain, post-traumatic stress disorder, or glaucoma. The researchers did identify data showing that cannabinoids could have a positive impact on sleep. But the small size of these studies and the fact that examining this connection was not the main objective of the investigations somewhat limits the usefulness of the findings. Furthermore, THC and CBD are vastly different, which makes any reference to cannabinoids confusing and unhelpful.

A survey of 4,637 ninth through twelfth graders in Colorado found that those who consumed cannabis through edibles or vaping tended to sleep fewer than seven hours per night. [^259] Another study of adolescents found that the sedative effects of THC were followed by increased wakefulness at night and impaired memory the next day, which could have been directly due to the THC, which is known to impair memory, lack of sleep, or both. [^260]

Researchers have also found a potential link between use of cannabis among pregnant mothers and poor sleep habits among their children during adolescence. [^261] You might be asking, “How many pregnant women use cannabis?” A recent report said that anywhere from 4 to 12 percent of pregnant mothers in the US said they’d used cannabis during pregnancy, usually by edible and usually in the first trimester prior to learning they were pregnant. [^262] Cannabis use during pregnancy has reportedly increased in recent years, from 3.4 percent in 2002 to 7 percent in 2017. [^263] Smoking or ingesting cannabis during pregnancy has been tied to lower birth weight, possibly due to THC-induced changes to the placenta. [^264] Rates of neonatal and infant death are higher with cannabis use during pregnancy compared to no such use (and combining cannabis with nicotine raises this risk even higher). [^265]

Many people use CBD to try to induce sleep, but rigorous evidence of a direct benefit to sleep is currently insufficient. Chances are any positive effects of CBD on sleep are due to its anxiety-lowering effects. CBD may help people to stop ruminating—a prerequisite to falling asleep. As such, there are populations for whom CBD may be useful. In one study, fifty-seven of seventy-two adults with anxiety reported improved sleep with the use of CBD, although this study was retrospective, meaning the participants were reporting their recall of possible effects from memory rather than measuring them directly. [^266] A 2025 review of twenty-nine studies identified a potential for CBD to reduce sleep disruptions but emphasized that research on this link has suffered from a lack of standardization. [^267] There certainly is enough evidence to warrant continued study of CBD in this context and no known negative effects of CBD that would preclude trying it for sleep if you feel stressed at night. That said, in January 2024, a team from Australia published the results of a small, randomized, placebo-controlled study in which fifteen people received 150 milligrams of CBD and fifteen people received a placebo as a sleep aid to combat insomnia. [^268] The investigators observed no difference between the two groups in the time it took to fall asleep, the efficiency of their sleep, the duration of sleep, or overall severity of insomnia. There were some signs of an improved mood upon waking among the CBD group, and that group had fewer night wakings after two weeks of treatment.
One more thing: An increasing number of studies report a potential for THC (but not CBD) to induce psychosis in certain individuals. [^269]

If your goal is to improve your sleep, there are better tools covered in the other protocols of this chapter. The same goes for stress management—more reliable tools exist (and these can improve sleep too), which I’ll explain in a later chapter.
SLEEP PROTOCOL 14 Avoid Screens Within an Hour or More Before Bedtime
WHAT TO DO
• Avoid screens in the bedroom at night. This includes phones, laptops, tablets, and TV screens.
• Avoid consuming information on an electronic device within an hour (at least) of bedtime. Light from phones and other screens can disrupt your circadian clock.

• If you opt to read or watch content on a screen in the hour before sleep, dim the screen. I suggest lowering the brightness and/or activating the “red” screen function. You can also wear blue and green (short wavelength) blocking glasses.
HOW IT WORKS

In 2011, the National Sleep Foundation conducted a poll. [^270] They asked 1,508 Americans about their sleep habits, whether any technology was around them in the hour before bed, and if so, what it was and how they used it. Ninety percent of respondents said they used some kind of screen device at this time; for those under thirty, that percentage climbed to 96! Adolescent and young adult respondents were more likely to use cell phones or play video games before bed compared to adults over thirty, and the same went for computers and digital music players. I strongly suspect those percentages have either held constant or increased in the last decade and a half. In 2011, watching television was the most common activity among the entire sample. Others included doing homework, using social media, using a smartphone, sending work emails, and other activities. The researchers also asked about reading printed books and magazines before bed, which about half of respondents reported doing.

More than half the respondents—63 percent, to be exact—said they didn’t get enough sleep on weeknights. And nearly all the people who reported insufficient sleep said it negatively affected both their personal and professional lives. The high rates of late-night technology use and insufficient sleep seen in the survey responses didn’t automatically mean the two were related, so the researchers conducted some statistical analyses to check for such a link. They found that difficulty falling asleep rose in keeping with the amount of technology people used in the hour before bed. More passive devices like e-readers were less problematic than interactive devices like game consoles, cell phones, and laptops.

These screens are illuminated by LEDs, and as we’ve discussed in this chapter, this type of lighting is disruptive to our circadian rhythm. Evidence suggests that LED screens can interrupt melatonin production, which, as you now know, is essential for sleep. In 2014, a group of sleep researchers at Harvard Medical School reported that people who read on an e-book at night with a dim bedside light took longer to fall asleep, were less sleepy, had lower levels of melatonin, and were less alert the next morning compared to people who read a printed book with a dim bedside light before bed. [^271]

And there’s more. In 2018, a team of researchers, including UCLA psychiatrist Peter Whybrow, reviewed the data on the potential link between LED lighting and mental health. [^272] They concluded that exposure to blue light, in particular, posed a risk to sleep and other processes governed by the circadian system. There is also evidence suggesting that the way in which artificial lighting at night interferes with this system may lead to depression. [^273]

The problem with devices at bedtime is not solely due to the type of lighting. Technology, particularly interactive technology, stimulates our brains in a way that counters the calm that we need in order to fall asleep. For example, the devices in the 2018 study were most strongly linked to difficulty falling asleep and to poor sleep quality. Also, people who sleep with their phones in their rooms with the ringer on contributed to the numbers reported in the study, indicating that the problem isn’t just about late-night scrolling.

We have known since at least the 1970s that the bedroom should be reserved for sleep and intimacy. [^274] The evidence linking various stimuli to insomnia is well established. Yet decades later, here we are, with about 1,350 out of 1,508 randomly selected Americans ignoring this basic practice.

Believe it or not (believe it!), this protocol is one of the most potent in this chapter. It’s also one of the most difficult to stick to for many people. Sleep-based apps and the use of smartphones as alarm clocks don’t make it any easier. Still: I highly suggest you try it.
COMMON QUESTIONS
Do blue-blocking glasses counter the negative effects of screens at night

Yes, somewhat. Better, however, would be glasses that block both blue and green light, aka short wavelengths of visible light, at that time—especially if you use screens at night. (See Sleep Protocol 3 for more information.)
SLEEP PROTOCOL 15 A Tip Sheet for Avoiding Jet Lag

Some people experience terrible jet lag, others far less so. This changes as we age. And it depends on where we fly—which direction and if we need to push ourselves to wake earlier or stay awake later than usual. The latter is always easier for people.

Five factors allow you to shift your circadian clock. Knowing these can help you switch to a new time zone quickly, which allows you to be more effective on work trips and enjoy vacations more fully. The factors you use to entrain your SCN to a new local light-dark cycle are, in descending order of influence:
• Light
• Temperature
• Meal times
• Exercise
• Social factors

You might think: Can’t I just hop on the local schedule? Alas, that’s hard because your SCN is entrained to wherever you have been for the prior week or so before your trip. So for instance if you fly from California to London and arrive at 5:00 p.m. and you view the sunset, your SCN thinks it’s morning sunlight and it wakes you up. But there is a way to overcome this. I’ll explain.
WHAT TO DO
BEFORE YOU TRAVEL EAST

Eastward travel is typically more challenging for the body. Why? Most people find it easier to stay awake later than to fall asleep earlier. But you can prepare for your trip and partially adjust your circadian rhythm before you leave:

• Get early bright light exposure, but be careful when. When traveling east, you need to shift to waking up earlier than you normally would. Starting two days before you leave, try waking up thirty to forty-five minutes prior to your usual wake-up time and view bright sunlight or bright artificial light as soon as you wake up.
• Drink caffeine early. This will help promote alertness early in the day and make it much easier to shift to your new time zone when you travel.
• Get moving. Within sixty minutes of your new, earlier wake-up time, exercise. Even just some light jogging will help if you can’t do a full workout.
These three levers—light, caffeine, and exercise—will help adjust your circadian clock to your new eastward-of-typical location, fast.
BEFORE YOU TRAVEL WEST

As mentioned earlier, westward travel tends to be easier for most people. That said, it can still help to adjust your circadian rhythm before you leave by using light, exercise, and caffeine. In this case, however, you’ll want to shift everything thirty to forty-five minutes later in the day as opposed to earlier. A slightly later wake-up time, a slightly later caffeine intake in the morning and early afternoon (but still avoid caffeine in the eight to ten hours prior to bedtime), and a slightly later workout—even just by forty-five minutes—will all help.
You’ll also want to make sure that you view bright light from artificial lights one to two hours after sunset. Remember, you’re trying to prepare to stay up later as you soon fly westward.
WHEN YOU ARRIVE AT YOUR NEW DESTINATION (REGARDLESS OF WHETHER YOU FLEW EAST OR WEST)

• Eat like a local. Adopting the local meal schedule when you arrive—eating breakfast, lunch, and dinner more or less at the same times as the locals, even if you’re not hungry—will help you shift your circadian clock to the new time zone. Personally, I hate to eat when I’m not hungry (and love to eat when I am!), so I opt out of this protocol. If it works for you, go for it. The sooner you can get on the local meal schedule, the better. Many find it effective to fast for a period of fourteen to sixteen hours before the local breakfast time so they are very hungry when that time arrives.

• Time your light exposure correctly by knowing your temperature minimum. This is the real power tool to shift your circadian clock fast, but it involves learning your temperature minimum first. See Sleep Protocol 3 and Sleep Protocol 5 for more on that topic. For now, know that it occurs approximately two hours before your usual wake-up time. If you typically wake up at 7:00 a.m., your temperature minimum is very likely to be between 4:30 a.m. and 5:30 a.m. Here’s the key: If you get bright light exposure in the one to two hours after your temperature minimum, you will adjust your circadian clock such that it will make you want to go to sleep earlier on the subsequent nights and wake up earlier on the subsequent mornings. Perfect for traveling east. Conversely, if you get bright light exposure in the one to two hours before your temperature minimum, you will shift your circadian clock such that it will make you want to go to sleep later on the subsequent nights and wake up later on the subsequent mornings. Perfect for traveling west. But remember we are referring to the time of your temperature minimum before you leave! This is vital to understand. Get it right and you’ll shift fast across time zones. Get it wrong and it can be a mess. Why? Well, think about this. Imagine you fly from San Francisco to London (+8 hours). You land in the morning London time and the sun is out. I said get morning sunlight in your eyes, right? Yes, but for the first two to three days in London before you adjust your clock, viewing that London morning sunlight is the same to your brain’s clock as getting a giant blast of light in your eyes at midnight San Francisco time. So you just made your body want to go to bed much later and wake up later. You got it backward. Many people sleep well their first night after flying east, wake up, see sunlight, and the second night is a mess. They can’t sleep! It would be better to wear dark sunglasses during the two to three hours before your temperature minimum for the first two days in London. After those first two or three days, just view sunlight per the recommendations earlier in this chapter. Obviously, I am just using London as an example. You must figure it out based on your own travel destination. I know it sounds complicated, but if you know the time of your temperature minimum back home, and follow the instructions above, you’ll nail this protocol easily.

• Use artificial light and blue and green (short wavelength) blocking glasses as tools. Of course, it’s often very cloudy, or you may land at night, and we can’t control the time of sunrise and sunset—though if you can, please contact me. What you can do, however, is travel with a portable bright light device (you’ll want one with 5,000- to 10,000-lux brightness) to shift your circadian clock. Several are the size of a book and thin enough to fit in a carry-on bag. I have no affiliation with any companies that make these, but I use the Verilux Happy Light when I travel. They cost about $50. At home I use a larger countertop unit, the Carex Daylight (also no affiliation) and Ra Optics or Bon Charge full-spectrum LED bulbs in the daytime, as discussed earlier. Remember that even when it is cloudy, sunlight through cloud cover is still almost always far brighter than artificial lighting. Get outside and view that sunlight at the correct times and you’ll shift your circadian clock fast. Then, you can return to the standard protocols to stay on the local schedule. One more thing we can all control is the brightness of our evening and nighttime environment. As you get ready for bed, reduce exposure to bright lights—especially blue and green, or short-wavelength, light. Alas, as you now know, all LED lights are rich in blue and green wavelengths. For that reason, I wear blue and green (short wavelength) blocking glasses after sundown to help adjust to the local schedule. This protocol is known to protect against the melatonin-reducing effects of bright light and to prevent the cortisol-increasing effects of bright light.
• Maintain a regular exercise schedule. While traveling, try to maintain a consistent early-in-the-day exercise routine (adjusted to the local schedule). That, too, helps shift your circadian clock.

• A final tip. For trips that last fewer than two days, staying on (or near) your home sleep-wake, eating, and exercise schedule can be beneficial to minimize disruptions to your circadian rhythm. These tips will help you quickly overcome any jet lag in your future travels—they’ve certainly helped me over the years, as well as people in the military, medical professions working night shifts, and more.
